justification: This is a rigorous, well-sourced article that beats both competing pages checked for "sorting algorithms": GeeksforGeeks's hub page has no complexity derivations, no runnable code, no citations, and no discussion of what a real stdlib sort does internally; Wikipedia asserts the Ω(n log n) bound with a citation but never derives it, has no runnable code, and treats stability only conceptually. This article derives the decision-tree lower bound and verifies it with an exhaustive 8!-permutation program, implements and measures all five algorithms, empirically verifies stability instead of asserting it, and grounds the .NET section in dotnet/runtime source rather than just the docs summary. I independently re-verified every quoted sentence against algs4.cs.princeton.edu (elementary sorts, mergesort, quicksort, priority queues), learn.microsoft.com (Array.Sort, List<T>.Sort, Enumerable.OrderBy), and the actual dotnet/runtime source (ArraySortHelper.cs, Array.cs) — all quotes are verbatim-accurate, and I hand-traced the n=3 decision tree in Figure 3 against the article's own InsertionSort code and confirmed the '[3,1,4]→102 in 2 comparisons' claim exactly. I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs` on the article myself (PASS, blocks=28, executed=14) and additionally recompiled the lower-bound program standalone via `dotnet run` to check its printed 40,320-permutation statistics. Two things keep this out of the 8.5+ band despite that strength: the 'Measure it: how close does Array.Sort get to 2n ln n?' exercise draws a causal conclusion its own data undercuts (see issue 1) — a factual/analytical error, which per the rubric caps the score at 7 — and the article never states a runtime/OS/CPU toolchain near its seeded-Random measurements, a binding pilot-round rule that previously cost other articles their pass, which matters concretely here because several blocks depend on `new Random(seed)` sequences. Two smaller issues (an avoidable wildcard, a missing crosslinks file) round this out. With those fixed this would credibly clear 8.5.

issues.location: Final exercise, 'Measure it: how close does Array.Sort get to 2n ln n?' (solution block, near the end of the article, just before 'Choosing a sort')
issues.problem: The solution states Array.Sort 'beats the plain-quicksort prediction by 20 to 30 percent at every size... consistent with median-of-three picking a better pivot than a random element would.' This overstates median-of-three's effect because the baseline it beats (~2n ln n) is Sedgewick & Wayne's leading-order asymptotic term, not the exact average comparison count for a plain random-pivot quicksort. I re-derived the exact formula C_n = 2(n+1)H_n − 4n (H_n = the n-th harmonic number) and computed it precisely: n=100 → 647.9, n=1000 → 10,985.9, n=10,000 → 155,771.7 (verified by direct computation, not estimation). Against this more precise baseline, Array.Sort's measured counts (631 / 10,202 / 146,439) are only about 2.6%, 7.1% and 6.0% lower — not 20-30%. Worse, the article's own earlier 'quicksort-cost' block already contradicts the causal story: its naive last-element-pivot quicksort with NO median-of-three, run on the same n=1000 after a Fisher–Yates shuffle (seed 7), measured 10,134 comparisons — fewer than Array.Sort's 10,202 for the same n, and it beats the crude ~2n ln n prediction by essentially the same 26.6% the exercise attributes to median-of-three (Array.Sort's own gap there is 26.2%). A plain shuffled quicksort with no median-of-three and no insertion-sort fallback shows the same 'beat' from the same article's own data, so the 20-30% figure is mostly an artifact of comparing to a loose asymptotic formula, not evidence that median-of-three is responsible for it.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either (a) compare Array.Sort's measured counts against the exact C_n = 2(n+1)H_n − 4n baseline instead of ~2n ln n, and report the real, smaller advantage (roughly 3-8% at these sizes) attributable to median-of-three plus the insertion-sort fallback for small partitions, or (b) explicitly note that the naive shuffled quicksort earlier in the article shows a comparable 'beat' over the crude baseline with no median-of-three at all, and reframe the exercise's conclusion around that comparison instead of asserting causation the article's own numbers don't support.

issues.location: Article-wide — no toolchain statement anywhere, including next to the seeded-Random blocks (quicksort-cost id=quicksort-cost, its 'Measure it' exercise using Random(1)/Random(2)/Random(3), the Array.Sort/OrderBy stability demo using Random(5), and the final exercise using Random(11))
issues.problem: docs/EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md's binding 'Lessons from the pilot round' require stating the toolchain once, near where measurements appear ('.NET 10.0.x on Windows 11, x64 laptop', in the writer's own words). I grepped the full article text for '.NET 10', 'Windows', 'x64', 'CPU' etc.; the only hits are the front-matter description (a generic claim about what Array.Sort/OrderBy run 'in .NET 10', not a stated toolchain) and the phrase 'on this machine' (line ~497), which names no version. This matters specifically here, not generically: `Random`'s algorithm changed in .NET 6, so every seeded sequence in this article (comparison counts, ticket orderings, the Array.Sort-vs-OrderBy stability demo) is runtime-version-dependent, and a reader on a different major version could get different numbers than the ones printed.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one sentence near the first seeded-Random block (or once, near the top of the quicksort section) stating the exact runtime, OS and CPU class used to produce every seeded/measured number in the article, in prose (not a stamped opening line — the site already states that globally per the same rule).

issues.location: 'No comparison sort can beat n log n comparisons' section, the id=lower-bound code block's output (`min comparisons: [...]`, `max comparisons: [...]`, `average: [...]`)
issues.problem: These three values are wildcarded as if they were machine-dependent, but they are not: they are an exhaustive count over all 8! = 40,320 permutations of a fixed, deterministic merge-sort implementation, so they are exactly reproducible on any machine (unlike the seeded-Random timing/shuffle values elsewhere, which legitimately vary). I compiled and ran the exact program standalone via `dotnet run` and got min=12, max=17, average=15.733 every time. Hiding these throws away the article's best remaining proof point: max=17 is only one comparison above the proven floor of 16 for n=8, which would be a much stronger, concrete demonstration of how tight this specific merge-sort implementation is to the Ω(n log n) bound than the current 'it sits inside the [12, 24] Sedgewick range' framing.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace the three `[...]` lines with the real numbers (min comparisons: 12, max comparisons: 17, average: 15.7) and add a sentence noting the worst case (17) is within one comparison of the proven floor (16) for n=8.
